title: Outside Time
summary: Daytime outdoor light by morning, peak sun, or afternoon—full sun or shade, with duration—separate from the Sunrise check-in.

sections.heading: What Outside Time is
sections.body: Outside Time is the daytime outdoor-light habit: you go outdoors after the sunrise slot and log when, whether you were in full sun or shade, and how long you stayed. It is not the Sunrise check-in. Sunrise unlocks the day boost from morning eye light; Outside Time tracks the rest of the solar day for skin, spectrum, and place-timed UV.

sections.heading: Why one activity, three slots
sections.body: Morning, peak sun, and afternoon are different jobs. Place sun times route each log: morning from sunrise until 1.5 hours before solar noon; peak sun for the symmetrical ±1.5-hour window around solar noon (the UVB-centered band); afternoon from then until sunset. Peak sun is where vitamin D synthesis is most efficient per minute when season allows. Morning and afternoon still train outdoor spectrum and movement—just with different UV profiles.

sections.heading: Practical habit
sections.body: Step outside on purpose. Prefer full sun when safe and non-burning; shade still counts at lower points. Build duration gradually. Glass does not count as outside. Pair peak-sun logs with the solar-noon vitamin D lesson when repletion is your goal. Log another session anytime you go out again in a different slot.

sections.heading: What is solid vs framework
sections.body: Solid ground: outdoor daylight differs from indoor LEDs in intensity and spectrum; solar noon UVB matters for vitamin D; non-burning exposure is the safe pattern. Framework: that every shaded minute is worthless, or that Outside Time replaces sunrise eye light. They are complementary—eyes at dawn, skin and day spectrum through Outside Time.

sections.heading: How to use it here
sections.body: Log Outside Time: choose morning, peak sun, or afternoon, full sun or shaded, and duration. Sunrise check-in stays separate. Read Solar noon sun for vitamin D for the peak-sun skin story. Educational only—not dermatology or burn guidance; respect your skin type and clinician advice.
